evidence.label: Unbounded Violations of the Square-Root Degree Bound

headline: Boolean functions can beat the proposed square-root-of-degree bound on their linear correlations by any factor.
scope: Applies to functions from n inputs of ±1 to outputs of ±1; the number of inputs needed is finite but not bounded usefully.
plain: A Boolean function turns n inputs of +1 or −1 into one output of +1 or −1. Gopalan and Servedio conjectured that its total agreement with single inputs is at most a constant times the square root of its degree. This paper proves that false. For any constant, some function exceeds the proposed bound by that factor.
doesNot: This does not say how many inputs are needed for a given violation, or what the true growth rate is.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It refutes a known conjecture in the analysis of Boolean functions by an unbounded factor.

explanation:
Take three yes-or-no votes, written as +1 or −1. Let f be the majority vote: it outputs whichever sign has at least two votes. How much does f agree with each single voter? On average over all 8 vote patterns, f times voter 1 equals 1/2. The same holds for voters 2 and 3. So the three agreements add up to 3/2.

A Boolean function here takes n inputs, each +1 or −1, and outputs +1 or −1. The agreement with voter i is called the i-th linear Fourier coefficient. Every such function can be written as a polynomial in its inputs. Its degree is the largest number of inputs multiplied together in any term. Majority on three votes has degree 3, because it equals (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/2 − x₁x₂x₃/2.

A simple argument bounds the sum of the linear coefficients by √n[1]. Gopalan and Servedio conjectured that √n could be replaced by the square root of the degree[2]. The conjecture is attributed to them around 2009[4]. For majority on three votes, the sum is 1.5 and √3 is about 1.73. So that example fits. A stronger guess compared every function with majority itself[5]. Kudin and Pašalić refuted that stronger guess at degree 4[6]. The square-root version stayed open.

This paper proves the square-root version false, and badly so[3]. For any number C, however large, it finds a Boolean function whose linear sum exceeds C times the square root of its degree. No fixed multiple of the proposed bound can hold. A weaker bound does survive: the sum is never more than the degree itself[7]. So the truth lies somewhere between the square root and the degree.

The difficulty is to get large agreement while keeping the degree low. The paper first builds a function that reports partial information about many independent scores. Each part of its output is a polynomial of small degree. Yet together these parts keep more information about the total than their degree would suggest. The saving comes from terms cancelling, not from ignoring some input[9]. Repeating this step pushes the ratio up without limit.

There is a limit to what this gives. The functions exist and have finitely many inputs. But the paper does not give useful bounds on how many inputs it needs[8]. So it does not say how fast the ratio can grow with the number of inputs.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the main result. The Lean scope note covers every C. For each, it gives a nonconstant Boolean function whose linear sum exceeds C times the square root of its degree. It also covers the version with absolute values. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid. Lean has checked the main statement; no specialist review is published, and the size of the examples is not controlled.
